records.sourceFile: London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries Part 3 - Rehabilitation, running and return to sport.pdf

paper.citation: Paton BM, Read P, van Dyk N, Wilson MG, Pollock N, Court N, et al. London International Consensus and Delphi study on hamstring injuries part 3: rehabilitation, running and return to sport. Br J Sports Med. 2023.
paper.abstract: A modified Delphi process with an international expert panel produced consensus statements on hamstring injury rehabilitation, running and return to sport. The panel recommends individualised rehabilitation based on sporting demands, the involved muscle and injury severity, with pain-free sprinting, running progression and a multidisciplinary, athlete-involved return-to-sport process. Agreement was not reached on flexibility and strength benchmarks or on adjuncts such as blood flow restriction.
paper.tldr: An international expert panel agreed that hamstring rehabilitation should be individualised to sporting demands, muscle and injury type, and that running, sprinting and an athlete-involved return-to-sport process are central. Benchmarks for flexibility and strength, and the use of adjuncts such as blood flow restriction, were not agreed.
paper.methods: This was a modified Delphi study with a literature review. Round 1 was an open-ended survey of 46 invited experts (35 responded), a consensus meeting of 15 experts drafted statements with facilitated debate and anonymous voting, and a round 2 online survey of 99 respondents (of 112 invited) voted true, false or undecided. The threshold was 70% agreement, and athletes were not included as survey participants.
paper.findings: Statements reaching 70% or more included that the order and speed of exercise progression should depend on the adaptation required (96.2%), symptoms (88.9%) and stage of tissue healing (90.7%), that on-pitch running is a significant part of rehabilitation (98.4%) and that running dosage should be increased to full sprinting (100%). Pain-free running was agreed as a criterion for sprinting (85.5%) and pain-free sprinting as a criterion for return to play (96.7%), and a full unrestricted training session (93.3%) and a multidisciplinary return-to-sport process involving all stakeholders (98.3%) were also supported. Agreement was not reached for flexibility as a progression criterion (67.9%), range of motion as a return-to-sport consideration (45.0%), strength benchmarks within 10% (66.1%), the Askling H-test (57.6%) or adjuncts such as blood flow restriction (68.9%), all values from Tables 1 to 3.
paper.limitations: The meeting included 15 of 35 round 1 respondents, women were few (Table 4 gives 2 of 35, 1 of 15 and 18 of 99, while the text says 2 of 39 in round 1), no athletes were included, and experts from Asia, Africa and South America could not attend. Several figures conflict within the paper: the abstract gives 88.2% for round 2 response (99 of 112 is 88.4%) and 40% for flexibility benchmarks (Table 3 gives 45.0%), and the discussion gives 67.8% for adjuncts, 56.1% for the Askling H-test and 98.6% for athlete apprehension where the tables give 68.9%, 57.6% and 98.3%; table values are reported here. The authors note that the background rehabilitation literature is small (six studies with about 386 athletes) and heterogeneous.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should individualise hamstring rehabilitation to the sport's demands, the injured muscle and the tissue type, and should progress loading by symptoms, healing stage and response to previous loading. Running and sprinting should be included in late rehabilitation, with pain-free sprinting before return to play and a full training session as a criterion. Benchmarks for flexibility and strength, and adjuncts such as blood flow restriction, should not be treated as agreed standards.
paper.athleteDev: The panel supports building running and sprinting dosage toward game-level intensities and volumes before return to play, and using GPS data to guide running load. The consensus does not give specific load, speed or sprint-volume thresholds.
paper.rtp: The panel's criteria include pain-free sprinting, a full unrestricted training session, peak isometric and eccentric strength at length and athlete self-assessment, decided by a multidisciplinary team. The consensus did not establish validated return-to-sport tests, strength benchmarks or reinjury rates, so it cannot set a fixed return-to-sport timeline.

records.sourceFile: Longitudinal changes in quadriceps morphology over the first 3 months after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.pdf

paper.citation: Johnston CD, Dewig DR, Pietrosimone B, Padua D, Ryan ED, Hart J, et al. Longitudinal Changes in Quadriceps Morphology over the First 3 Months after Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2024;56(5):933-941.
paper.abstract: This prospective cohort compared quadriceps echo intensity (a marker of poorer muscle quality) and cross-sectional area in 20 people with ACL reconstruction and 12 healthy controls at baseline, 1 month and 3 months. Echo intensity was higher in the ACLR limb than baseline and the contralateral limb at 1 and 3 months, while muscle size fell and then increased from 1 to 3 months without a matching change in echo intensity. The authors conclude that muscle quality declines rapidly after ACLR and does not recover within 3 months.
paper.tldr: Quadriceps muscle quality, measured by ultrasound echo intensity, worsened within the first month after ACL reconstruction and did not improve by 3 months, even as muscle size began to recover. From 1 to 3 months size and quality changed independently, so size alone may not show the full picture.
paper.methods: Prospective cohort in which 20 people with ACL reconstruction (15 men, 5 women) and 12 healthy controls were tested before surgery or at baseline, at 1 month and at 3 months, with 32 of 54 recruited completing all sessions. Ultrasound images of the vastus lateralis and rectus femoris were used to calculate echo intensity, corrected for subcutaneous fat, and anatomical cross-sectional area, and mixed-model ANOVAs compared the ACLR limb with controls and with the contralateral limb.
paper.findings: In the ACLR limb, echo intensity increased from baseline at 1 month (vastus lateralis +11.45%, rectus femoris +9.83%) and at 3 months (+11.50% and +9.40%), with no change between 1 and 3 months. Vastus lateralis cross-sectional area fell 25.1% at 1 month and rose 17.9% from 1 to 3 months, while rectus femoris area returned to baseline by 3 months; the baseline to 1 month changes in size and echo intensity were correlated for the vastus lateralis (r = -0.584, P = 0.007) but not the rectus femoris, and no changes were correlated from 1 to 3 months. Echo intensity did not differ significantly between the ACLR and control groups at any time point (Bonferroni-adjusted alpha 0.006), although the differences exceeded the control-derived minimal clinically important difference at 1 and 3 months.
paper.limitations: The sample is small: 32 of 54 recruited participants (20 of 30 ACLR, 12 of 24 controls) completed all three visits, and the COVID-19 pandemic stopped the planned 6-month assessment. The abstract states that changes in quality and size were not correlated, but the results report a significant first-month correlation for the vastus lateralis, and the Figure 5 caption says the ACLR limb did not differ from control while the text reports smaller vastus lateralis area than controls at 1 and 3 months. Echo intensity may be affected by hydration and probe orientation, rehabilitation was not standardized, control-group physical activity was not measured, only the vastus lateralis and rectus femoris were imaged, and no strength or functional outcome was reported.
paper.practicalImplications: Clinicians may consider tracking echo intensity alongside muscle size during early rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction, since size recovered from 1 to 3 months while echo intensity did not. The findings do not show that current rehabilitation should change, and the authors state that further work is needed on how to reverse the shift in muscle composition.
paper.athleteDev: The study did not measure strength, power or performance, so it does not show what this muscle quality change means for an athlete's training or load decisions.
paper.rtp: The study covers the first 3 months after ACL reconstruction and reports no return-to-sport criteria or outcomes. It cannot be used to judge readiness to return to sport, though the authors suggest echo intensity could give an objective progress marker that size measures do not.

records.sourceFile: Low prevalence of cardiac abnormalities in competitive athletes at return to play after COVID-19.pdf

paper.citation: Maestrini V, Penza M, Filomena D, Birtolo LI, Monosilio S, Lemme E, et al. Low prevalence of cardiac abnormalities in competitive athletes at return-to-play after COVID-19. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2022.
paper.abstract: In 219 competitive athletes evaluated for return to play after COVID-19, all had good exercise capacity and normal echocardiographic systolic and diastolic function. Two cases of acute myocarditis (0.9%) were found on cardiac MRI, and uncommon premature ventricular contractions were found in about 9% of athletes. The authors conclude that exercise testing has additional value in return-to-play evaluation, but the study had no comparison group and was not designed to measure the yield of CPET or Holter.
paper.tldr: Among 219 competitive athletes screened for return to play after COVID-19, 0.9% had myocarditis on cardiac MRI and about 9% had uncommon ventricular ectopy at exercise testing. The study had no control group, so these figures describe one screening protocol rather than the risk caused by infection.
paper.methods: Single-centre cross-sectional study of competitive athletes evaluated between October 2020 and May 2021 before resuming training, using the Italian return-to-play protocol: 12-lead ECG, blood tests including high-sensitivity troponin, pulmonary function, transthoracic echocardiography, maximal symptom-limited CPET, and 24-hour Holter ECG. Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement and T1/T2 mapping was performed on clinical indication. Results are descriptive; no control group was included.
paper.findings: Of 219 athletes (59% male, median age 23), none had cardiovascular or respiratory limitation on CPET, and echocardiography showed normal systolic and diastolic function in all. Uncommon PVCs were found at CPET in 20 athletes (9%), and 13 of the 16 with a prior evaluation (81%) had newly diagnosed arrhythmia after COVID-19. Two female athletes (0.9%) had acute myocarditis on CMR, with raised troponin and increased T1 and T2 mapping values. Five athletes (2%) were temporarily not eligible for sport and were followed up.
paper.limitations: Single centre, no comparison group, and pre-infection data for only about half the cohort. The authors state that a defined association between infection and arrhythmia cannot be proved. CMR was not performed in all athletes, so tissue abnormalities are likely undercounted. Several figures conflict: the abstract reports 9.5% (21 athletes) with ectopy at CPET or Holter, while the text reports 9% (20) at CPET; the abstract says three athletes were restricted from sport, while the results describe five; the abstract reports one new pericardial effusion, while echocardiography in the results shows mild effusion in four; and non-sustained VT is 1.4% in the text but 1.6% in Table 2.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors argue that CPET adds value to return-to-play screening after COVID-19, because the athletes withdrawn from sport had uncommon PVCs at CPET and Holter, but the study was not designed to measure the diagnostic yield of CPET or Holter and had no comparison group. Myocarditis was uncommon in this group, but the 0.9% figure should not be used as a general risk estimate. The authors suggest CMR when myocarditis is likely, such as with symptoms, suspicious findings or uncommon PVC morphology.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: Athletes showed good exercise capacity on CPET after recovery, with no functional limitation reported. The study did not measure training or performance outcomes, so it cannot show how training load should change after infection.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Two athletes with myocarditis were withdrawn, and two athletes with newly diagnosed uncommon PVCs were withdrawn temporarily and resumed about three months later when the arrhythmias had disappeared. The protocol is not validated outside this cohort, so the 0.9% figure should not be used as a clearance criterion, and because CMR was done only on clinical indication the study cannot show that a normal CPET or Holter excludes myocarditis.

records.sourceFile: Low rate of return to pre-injury sport level in athletes after cartilage surgery- a 10-year follow-up study.pdf

paper.citation: Zaffagnini S, Vannini F, Di Martino A, Andriolo L, Sessa A, Perdisa F, et al. Low rate of return to pre-injury sport level in athletes after cartilage surgery: a 10-year follow-up study. Knee Surgery, Sports Traumatology, Arthroscopy. 2018.
paper.abstract: In 31 competitive male athletes treated with arthroscopic MACT for focal knee cartilage lesions, IKDC scores improved markedly and stayed stable to 10 years. Overall, 64.5% returned to a competitive level and 58.1% to the same pre-injury level, with return rates falling over time. Previous surgery was the most influential factor for returning to the same level (p = 0.010), and the authors conclude that the chondrocyte-based approach has limits for sport-related outcomes.
paper.tldr: In 31 competitive male athletes treated with cartilage repair for knee lesions, clinical scores stayed improved for 10 years, but only about 3 in 10 were still at their pre-injury level at 10 years. Previous knee surgery, degenerative or OCD lesions and higher BMI were linked to poorer sport return.
paper.methods: Prospective case series of 31 male competitive athletes (34 enrolled, 3 lost) with focal grade III to IV osteochondral lesions of the distal femur, treated with arthroscopic hyaluronan-based MACT between 2000 and 2006. Patients completed IKDC subjective, Tegner and EQ-VAS scores before surgery and yearly for up to 10 years. Return to sport was recorded by competitive level (Tegner 8 to 10) and by pre-injury level, and factors were examined with Friedman, Mann-Whitney, ANOVA and backward logistic regression. No control group was included.
paper.findings: IKDC subjective score rose from 40.3 +/- 13.4 to 81.7 +/- 14.4 at 12 months, 89.5 +/- 11.3 at 2 years and 87.3 +/- 13.6 at 10 years. The Tegner score rose from 1.9 pre-treatment to 6.7 +/- 2.3 at 10 years, which remained below the pre-injury mean of 9.1 +/- 2.3. Return to a competitive level was 61.3%, 45.2% and 35.5% at 2, 5 and 10 years, and return to the same pre-injury level was 54.8%, 38.7% and 29.0%. Return to competitive level was 84% without previous surgery and 33% with it (p = 0.007), 87% for traumatic lesions versus 33% for degenerative and 50% for OCD lesions (p = 0.035), and 92.3% in athletes under 20; higher BMI was also linked to lower return (p = 0.001). In multivariate analysis previous surgery and BMI were the factors retained. Only one failure was recorded, in a 19-year-old who needed further surgery at 6 years.
paper.limitations: Uncontrolled series with 31 patients and level IV evidence, and no imaging assessment of the repaired tissue. The time to return is not reported in the results despite being listed as an outcome. The logistic regression odds ratios (for example 139.7 for previous surgery on competitive level) are unstable for this sample size. Comparisons with other studies (73% to 84% return rates) mix different populations and definitions. The title's 'low rate' refers to same-level return, while the abstract describes the outcome as satisfactory and the overall return to sport as successful. The surgery was performed 2000 to 2006 with a specific hyaluronan scaffold, so the 10-year data may not reflect current techniques.
paper.practicalImplications: Discuss realistic expectations before cartilage surgery: in this series about 6 in 10 athletes returned to competitive play at some point, but fewer than 3 in 10 were at their pre-injury level by 10 years. Previous surgery, degenerative or OCD lesions, older age and higher BMI were linked to lower return, so these should shape counselling. Clinical scores can remain high while sport level falls, so staff should track sport level as well as symptom scores.
paper.athleteDev: Performance Application: The study measures sport level by the Tegner scale, not performance. It shows that competitive athletes' activity level stayed below pre-injury levels at 10 years (6.7 versus 9.1), but no performance metrics were recorded.
paper.rtp: Return to Sport Application: Around 58% of these athletes returned to their pre-injury level at some follow-up point, falling to 29% at 10 years. Previous surgery, degenerative or OCD lesions, older age and higher BMI were associated with lower return, so these factors should inform return-to-sport expectations. The results do not report time to return, so this study cannot set a timeline for return.

records.sourceFile: Managing lower limb muscle reinjuries in athletes - From risk factors to return to play strategies.pdf

paper.citation: Palermi S, Vittadini F, Vecchiato M, Corsini A, Demeco A, Massa B, et al. Managing Lower Limb Muscle Reinjuries in Athletes: From Risk Factors to Return-to-Play Strategies. J Funct Morphol Kinesiol. 2023;8:155.
paper.abstract: This narrative review covers the epidemiology, risk factors, clinical management, imaging, prevention and artificial intelligence applications for lower limb muscle reinjury, with a focus on football players. Reinjury is defined as recurrence of the same injury type at the same site within 2 months, or up to 1 year in other definitions.
paper.tldr: Muscle reinjury remains common, and the authors argue for a multidisciplinary plan that combines individualized rehabilitation, return criteria beyond elapsed time, eccentric training and training-load monitoring.
paper.methods: Narrative review of PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science literature, selected by keywords and by the authors' judgement of relevance, limited to peer-reviewed English-language articles. The authors state that, unlike systematic reviews, it does not follow a strict inclusion protocol or appraise study quality and risk of bias in depth.
paper.findings: Reinjury rates are reported as 12% to 43% across sports, with a meta-analysis cited for a risk ratio of 4.8 for recent hamstring strain. The authors describe eccentric exercise as having the strongest evidence for secondary prevention and cite an acute-to-chronic workload ratio of 0.8 to 1.3 as a target. They describe robust evidence for physical therapies and platelet-rich plasma as limited or elusive.
paper.limitations: The review may omit relevant studies and may not match the depth of systematic reviews, and the search window is not stated. Table 2 lists higher reinjury risk for high-grade muscle injuries, while the text cites Malliaropoulos et al. for higher reinjury risk after low-grade hamstring lesions, and the review does not reconcile the two.
paper.practicalImplications: Return-to-play decisions should combine clinical, strength, flexibility and sport-specific tests, because the authors argue that elapsed time alone can allow return before tissue maturity. Eccentric strengthening and training-load monitoring belong in prevention plans for athletes with prior muscle injury.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can include eccentric hamstring work and training-load monitoring in prevention planning for athletes with prior muscle injury. The review reports no performance outcome data.
paper.rtp: The review supports individualized return-to-training and return-to-play criteria based on clinical, strength and sport-specific tests rather than time alone. It gives no validated cut-off values and notes that no MRI finding has strong evidence for predicting reinjury at return, although one retrospective study linked some features to risk.

records.sourceFile: Maximum-Speed Single-Leg Bridge Test for Concentric Functional Assessment and Exercise in an Athlete with Recurrent Hamstring Strain Injuries - A Case Report.pdf

paper.citation: Sano Y, Kawabata M, Kenmoku T, Watanabe H, Takahira N. Maximum-Speed Single-Leg Bridge Test for Concentric Functional Assessment and Exercise in an Athlete with Recurrent Hamstring Strain Injuries: A Case Report. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2025;20(5):716-726.
paper.abstract: The authors describe a rugby player on a fourth hamstring strain recurrence, whose residual high-speed deficits were found by the maximum-speed single-leg bridge test. The same test was then used as a home intervention, with reported gains in speed, height, isometric knee flexor strength and flexibility, and ultrasound changes in the muscle.
paper.tldr: A high-speed single-leg bridge test identified deficits that conventional strength and flexibility tests did not, and the test was then used as a training exercise. For practitioners, this is a single-case signal that speed-based hamstring testing may be worth trialling in rehabilitation.
paper.methods: Single case of a 21-year-old rugby player with a fourth semitendinosus recurrence, tested monthly with the maximum-speed single-leg bridge test, VAS pain, active knee extension, isometric knee flexor strength and ultrasound. The test was then used as a two-month daily home exercise, with a 1.5-month detraining follow-up and compliance of 94.3% tracked by exercise videos.
paper.findings: At one month after injury there was no reported side-to-side difference in isometric knee flexor strength or flexibility, and at two months the injured side showed lower buttock-raising height (0.19 m vs 0.22 m) and speed (0.83 vs 1.01 m/s) than the uninjured side. After the two-month intervention, height was 0.35 m and speed 1.46 m/s, and both were largely maintained after 1.5 months of detraining (0.36 m, 1.36 m/s), with ultrasound showing fewer muscle fibre irregularities.
paper.limitations: The paper describes one athlete with no control group and a short follow-up, and the authors state it is uncertain whether resolving these deficits prevents recurrence. Because testing ran from two to four months after injury, the gains cannot be separated from natural healing. The injury involved the semitendinosus rather than the more commonly injured biceps femoris, and Table 1 lists Active Knee Extension values of 23.0 degrees uninjured versus 14.0 injured at one month although the text reports no flexibility difference.
paper.practicalImplications: A speed-based single-leg bridge test may reveal hamstring deficits that strength and flexibility tests miss in an athlete who has met standard criteria. Keep sets short enough to preserve high-speed movement, since the authors reduced the protocol after fatigue slowed movement speed and consistency.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff could add a high-speed hamstring test to monitoring for athletes with recurrent strain, since this case showed speed deficits that conventional tests missed. The authors compare the athlete with a reference average of 0.98 m/s from 26 healthy recreational athletes, but a single case cannot set norms.
paper.rtp: The authors suggest the test could become part of return-to-play criteria, because the athlete still had deficits after standard criteria were met. Its value for predicting re-injury is untested, so it should be used alongside established criteria, not in place of them.

records.sourceFile: Movement variability and loading characteristics in athletes with athletic groin pain - Changes after successful return to play and compared with uninjured athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Baida S, King E, Gore S, Richter C, Franklyn-Miller A, Moran K. Movement Variability and Loading Characteristics in Athletes With Athletic Groin Pain: Changes After Successful Return to Play and Compared With Uninjured Athletes. The Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine. 2022;10(10):23259671221125159.
paper.abstract: This laboratory study compared 36 athletes with athletic groin pain and 36 uninjured athletes during a continuous lateral hurdle hop, and retested the injured group after rehabilitation. At baseline the injured athletes had longer ground contact times and lower peak vertical ground reaction force, and these differences were no longer significant after rehabilitation.
paper.tldr: In a hurdle hop test, athletes with groin pain had longer ground contact and lower peak vertical force than controls, and these loading differences were no longer significant after rehabilitation. Movement variability did not differ at any point, and the authors suggest rehabilitation that targets trunk and pelvis control.
paper.methods: Pre- and post-rehabilitation laboratory cohort: 36 athletes with athletic groin pain were tested before and after a three-level exercise program focused on intersegmental control, and 36 uninjured athletes matched for age, level and sport were tested once. Each athlete made 10 continuous side-to-side hops over a 15 cm hurdle on force plates with 3D motion capture, and group comparisons used statistical parametric mapping, t tests and a permutation analysis of 30-athlete random samples.
paper.findings: At baseline, the groin pain group had longer ground contact time (P = .025, d = 0.43), greater concentric impulse (P = .028, d = 0.52) and lower peak vertical force (P = .025, d = 0.36) than controls; lower eccentric peak force (P = .029) and eccentric rate of force development (P = .049) were only trends that did not meet the 85% permutation criterion, and no movement variability or joint-level differences were found. From pre to post rehabilitation, the injured group's ground-force changes were not significant (small effect sizes), while trunk, pelvis and hip kinematics and hip kinetics changed significantly (for example, pelvic contralateral drop, d = -0.53). At return to play, ground-force measures no longer differed significantly from controls (ground contact time P = .755, peak force P = .589, concentric impulse P = .478).
paper.limitations: The uninjured group was tested only once and the injured group had no untreated comparison, so change over time, test familiarity and any rehabilitation effect cannot be separated. The abstract and discussion describe reduced rate of force development as a baseline finding, but the results report it as a trend that did not reach the 85% permutation criterion (P = .049, d = 0.34), and the pre-to-post ground-force changes were themselves non-significant; the abstract also gives a mean age of 27.5 years for the injured group where Table 1 gives 25.9. The rehabilitation was prescribed by two of the authors and the study was funded partly by the clinic.
paper.practicalImplications: Ground contact time and peak force from a continuous lateral hurdle hop on force plates differed between athletes with groin pain and controls at baseline, and the authors suggest that ground contact time, measurable with force plates or jump mats, may be a simple clinical measure; the within-group change in these measures after rehabilitation was not significant, so single-athlete change should be read cautiously. The authors suggest including trunk and pelvis control work during explosive, sport-specific movements, because pelvis and trunk kinematics changed with rehabilitation.
paper.athleteDev: For performance staff, athletes with groin pain had longer ground contact and lower peak force in a fast hop, and these differences were no longer significant after rehabilitation. The test was run in a laboratory with no training or competition outcomes, so it cannot show that these loading measures predict performance.
paper.rtp: Athletes were tested at return to play after clinical milestones were met, and their ground-force measures were no longer significantly different from controls, but this does not show equivalence and the study did not track re-injury or later sport participation. It cannot set return-to-play thresholds, and all HAGOS subscales except Symptoms, and the Marx activity score, remained significantly below the uninjured group at return.

records.sourceFile: Muscle activation during rehabilitation on artificial turf vs sand after cruciate ligament surgery - A case series.pdf

paper.citation: Rafols Parellada L, Linde X, Solà J, Fort A, Brau J. Muscle activation during rehabilitation on artificial turf vs. sand after cruciate ligament surgery: a case series. Apunts Sports Medicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: Describes surface EMG data from two female youth soccer players recovering from ACL surgery, recorded over six rehabilitation sessions on artificial turf and sand. The authors report increased activation of the cross pattern (left hamstring and right gluteus) in player 1 and of the left quadriceps in player 2, and conclude that the muscle most activated in both players was the antagonist of the injured leg, regardless of surface.
paper.tldr: Two case reports of ACL rehabilitation on turf and sand show surface EMG patterns that are worth describing but cannot yet guide practice. The authors themselves call for more cases before a common pattern is claimed.
paper.methods: Case series of two female youth soccer players after ACL surgery: player 1 had ACL and patellar tendon surgery on the left leg, and player 2 had ACL surgery with a semitendinosus plasty on the right leg. Surface EMG (Myontec Mbody AllSport 6-channel mesh) was recorded during six rehabilitation sessions, three on artificial turf and three on sand, for anterior and posterior chain muscles on both legs.
paper.findings: Player 1 showed higher left than right hamstring activation on five of six days, peaking at 36.7% on the first turf session. Player 2 showed higher left than right quadriceps activation on five of six days, with the largest difference (8.7 percentage points) on the first sand session. The authors conclude that the antagonist of the injured leg was the most active group in both players, regardless of surface.
paper.limitations: Two players, no statistics, and EMG values given as absolute percentages with no described normalisation. The text says player 1's left hamstring exceeded the right in all six posterior-chain sessions, but Table 1 shows the reverse on day 3, and the 'most active muscle is the antagonist' claim is not borne out in Table 1 on days 2, 3 and 5. Player 2's left quadriceps is called the antagonist of her injured leg, although her injured leg was the right.
paper.practicalImplications: Surface EMG on both legs can help staff describe muscle activity during ACL rehabilitation on different surfaces. Two cases cannot set a rehabilitation rule, so any surface choice should rest on the clinical picture and on more data.
paper.athleteDev: Does not measure performance. The sessions describe muscle activity during rehabilitation running on turf and sand in two players, with no performance outcome.
paper.rtp: Can describe muscle activity patterns during ACL rehabilitation on turf and sand, but cannot show that either surface improves return-to-play readiness. It contains no strength, hop or return-to-play criteria, so it cannot be used to clear an athlete to return to sport.

records.sourceFile: Neuromuscular training improves biomechanical deficits at the knee in ACL reconstructed athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Nagelli CV, Wordeman SC, Di Stasi S, Hoffman J, Marulli T, Hewett TE. Neuromuscular Training Improves Biomechanical Deficits at the Knee in Anterior Cruciate Ligament-Reconstructed Athletes. Clinical Journal of Sport Medicine. 2021;31(2):113-119.
paper.abstract: A cohort study of 18 athletes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) and 10 uninjured control athletes, all of whom completed a 12-session neuromuscular training program. Sagittal-plane knee biomechanics during drop vertical jumps improved in the ACLR group after training. After training, the groups had comparable sagittal-plane mechanics, and controls landed with a larger knee abduction angle than the ACLR athletes, who landed in slightly more adduction.
paper.tldr: Athletes after ACL reconstruction who completed a 12-session neuromuscular training program landed with a more flexed knee and lower flexion moment at initial contact during a drop jump. Frontal-plane knee measures did not change with training, and after training the ACLR athletes landed with less knee abduction than uninjured controls, not more.
paper.methods: Cohort study in a controlled laboratory. Athletes with ACLR (hamstring autograft, about 8 months post-surgery) and uninjured controls passed a clinical screen, and both groups completed 12 sessions of neuromuscular training in four phases. Knee kinematics and kinetics were recorded with 12-camera motion capture and force plates during three double-leg drop vertical jumps from a 30.5 cm box, before and after training in the ACLR group and after training in both groups, analysed with repeated-measures and two-way ANOVA.
paper.findings: In the ACLR group, knee flexion angle at initial contact increased from 17.2 to 24.3 degrees (session effect P=0.001), and knee flexion moment at initial contact decreased from 0.48 to 0.36 Nm/kg (P=0.008). Knee abduction angle and moment did not change significantly, limb symmetry for the sagittal variables did not change, and the uninvolved limb had a greater peak knee flexion moment than the involved limb (P=0.005). After training, controls had a larger knee abduction angle at initial contact than ACLR athletes, who landed in more adduction (group effect P=0.002), with no other group or limb effects.
paper.limitations: No untrained ACLR group was included, so the sagittal changes cannot be separated from time or natural recovery. The control group was small (n=10) and was analysed only after training. Screening excluded athletes with poor single-leg hop mechanics or joint effusion, so the cohort was higher functioning than typical, which the authors suggest may explain the lack of frontal-plane change. Exercise progression was based on trainer judgment, so athletes did not all complete the same exercises. The group means for knee abduction angle in the Results text and Table 3 do not match cleanly in the extracted text, so only the direction of the difference is reported here.
paper.practicalImplications: Rehabilitation and performance staff could consider a structured neuromuscular training program in the late stage of ACL rehabilitation to improve sagittal-plane landing mechanics, since knee flexion at landing increased. Frontal-plane measures did not change with training in this high-functioning cohort, which had been screened to exclude athletes with medial knee collapse, so the program's effect on valgus cannot be judged from this study.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff could use drop vertical jump knee flexion and flexion moment at initial contact to track landing mechanics in athletes returning from ACL reconstruction. The paper does not show that these landing changes improve sport performance.
paper.rtp: The study concerns athletes before return to sport and suggests neuromuscular training can improve sagittal-plane landing mechanics before return. It does not show that this program reduces second ACL injury, and the authors state that future work must test re-injury outcomes. Landing-mechanics improvement alone should not be used as a clearance criterion.

records.sourceFile: Neurosciences and Sports Rehabilitation in ACLR - A Narrative Review on Winning Alliance Strategies and Connecting the Dots.pdf

paper.citation: Calabro RS, Calderone A, Fiorente N. Neurosciences and Sports Rehabilitation in ACLR: A Narrative Review on Winning Alliance Strategies and Connecting the Dots. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2025;10:119.
paper.abstract: A narrative review of neuroplasticity, motor control and sensorimotor retraining in rehabilitation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR). The authors propose a conceptual model with three neuroplastic pathways and summarize robotics, virtual reality and biofeedback as tools to address neurocognitive deficits, with reinjury rates after ACLR of 9% to 29% in most studies cited. The review concludes that long-term monitoring and interdisciplinary work are needed.
paper.tldr: A narrative review argues that rehabilitation after ACL reconstruction should address brain-level changes, proprioception and fear of reinjury, not only strength. It proposes a conceptual model and summarizes technologies whose long-term effects, the authors say, are still being studied.
paper.methods: Narrative review of peer-reviewed literature from PubMed, Scopus and Web of Science, organised around a conceptual framework (the Neuroplastic Adaptation Trident Model) that the authors cite to Machan and Krupps (2021). Search terms, date limits and inclusion criteria are not reported, and study quality is not appraised or pooled.
paper.findings: The authors argue that ACL injury alters motor cortex activity, cerebellar and prefrontal activation, and proprioceptive processing, and they cite neuroimaging studies of ACLR patients. They cite a biofeedback study in young, physically active females (not stated to be ACLR patients) that reported a reduced peak knee abduction moment after six weeks, and a virtual reality study in which ACLR patients' knee biomechanics became more similar to healthy controls. Reported reinjury rates after ACLR range from 1.5% to 37.5%, with most studies reporting 9% to 29%.
paper.limitations: The review does not report search terms or inclusion criteria, and it does not appraise study quality. The authors acknowledge that robotic systems are costly and may not mimic multiplanar sport movements, that virtual reality can cause motion sickness, and that biofeedback needs skilled interpretation. They also state that long-term efficacy of these technologies remains under investigation.
paper.practicalImplications: Rehabilitation staff could add proprioceptive and dual-task drills, such as counting during drills or responding to unexpected cues, as the review suggests, while noting that much of this evidence comes from individual studies. The review also suggests biofeedback and force plate feedback for loading symmetry, but these need trained staff and equipment.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff could consider reaction and dual-task drills in the later phases after ACL reconstruction, as the review proposes. The review presents the link to athletic performance as a claim and does not provide performance outcome data.
paper.rtp: The review proposes neuroplasticity-based and cognitive-motor training as ways to reduce reinjury risk around return to play. It presents these within a conceptual framework rather than as tested criteria, and it states that long-term efficacy is still under investigation, so it should not be used to set return-to-play clearance.

records.sourceFile: No Association Between Fibrosis on Magnetic Resonance Imaging at Return to Play and Hamstring Reinjury Risk.pdf

paper.citation: Reurink G, Almusa E, Goudswaard GJ, Tol JL, Hamilton B, Moen MH, et al. No Association Between Fibrosis on Magnetic Resonance Imaging at Return to Play and Hamstring Reinjury Risk. The American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2015;43(5):1228-1234.
paper.abstract: In 108 athletes with grade 1 or 2 hamstring injuries, MRI fibrosis at return to play was present in 38% of athletes. Over one year, reinjury occurred in 24% of athletes both with and without fibrosis (HR 0.95, 95% CI 0.43 to 2.1), so fibrosis was not associated with reinjury in this cohort.
paper.tldr: Fibrosis on MRI at return to play was common after grade 1 or 2 hamstring injuries (38%), but it did not predict one-year reinjury (24% in both groups). With 26 reinjuries, the study could not detect a small or moderate association.
paper.methods: Cohort study pooling athletes from two double-blind randomized trials of platelet-rich plasma in hamstring injury, a Dutch cohort and a Qatari cohort, recruited from November 2009 to July 2014. MRI was performed within 5 days of injury and again within 1 week of return to play; each MRI was scored by one of two experienced radiologists, blinded to scan timing, for intramuscular low signal (fibrosis) on T1, T2 and fluid-sensitive images. Reinjury was recorded for one year and analysed with univariate and multivariable Cox proportional hazards models, the latter adjusted for prior ipsilateral hamstring injury and cohort.
paper.findings: Fibrosis was present at return to play in 41 of 108 athletes (38%), with a median longitudinal length of 5.8 cm. There were 26 reinjuries in total (19 of 63 in the Dutch cohort and 7 of 45 in the Qatari cohort). Reinjury occurred in 10 of 41 athletes with fibrosis (24%) and 16 of 67 without (24%), giving HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.43 to 2.1; P = .898). After adjustment, the HR was 1.3 (95% CI 0.55 to 2.8; P = .591).
paper.limitations: With 26 reinjuries the confidence interval (0.43 to 2.1) includes a doubling of risk, and the authors state only a moderate to strong association could be detected. The athletes came from platelet-rich plasma trials, the two cohorts used different MRI protocols and return-to-play criteria, fibrosis scoring had no reliability or histological data, and no MRI was done at reinjury. Two reporting conflicts: the abstract gives a fibrosis volume IQR of 1.5 to 3.9 cm3 while Table 3 gives 0.5 to 3.9 cm3 (Table 3 used here), and the Table 2 Qatari grade column repeats the whole-sample counts (45/63) although the Qatari cohort had 45 athletes.
paper.practicalImplications: Expect MRI fibrosis in about 4 in 10 athletes at return to play after grade 1 or 2 hamstring injuries; in this cohort it was not associated with reinjury, so it should not be treated alone as a reinjury marker. Because the study could only detect a moderate to strong association, it does not show that fibrosis is harmless, and it should not be used to set an MRI-based clearance rule either way.
paper.athleteDev: The study does not address training load or performance, so it gives no basis for changing training volume or intensity. Its only relevance is that fibrosis at return to play, which is common, was not associated with reinjury in these athletes.
paper.rtp: The study is directly about return to play after grade 1 or 2 hamstring injuries. Fibrosis was present in 38% of athletes at return to play (median 30 days after injury), and it was not associated with one-year reinjury here. It cannot identify a safe fibrosis threshold, cannot support clearance on MRI alone, and says nothing about grade 3 injuries.
